I'm looking for enthusiastic teammates with skills in software development, data analysis, UI/UX design, or geospatial technologies. Let's combine our strengths to build something creative and impactful!
summary:
FieldShift Mekong is a decision-support web app that helps Mekong Delta farmers and extension officers choose crop rotations for the next three seasons as salinity and drought intensify. A farmer draws their parcel on satellite imagery. FieldShift then simulates every feasible rotation day by day, using a FAO-56 soil-water balance driven by NASA POWER weather and initialised with POWER root-zone wetness. Each rotation is compared against the farmer's current sequence across 12 scenarios: climatology, dry, hot and early-salinity stress tests, an ENSO analog year built from NOAA ONI and NASA GPM IMERG rainfall, a seasonal forecast, and four NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 climate futures out to 2050.

For a coastal Sóc Trăng field facing the strong 2026–27 El Niño, the top strategy keeps the main winter–spring rice crop, sows it early and rests the saltiest season. This cuts the days crops stand in the salinity window from 177 to 84, and the strategy holds in 12 of 12 scenarios.

Every number shows its source, its uncertainty and what must be checked in the field first, such as canal water salinity. A weekly digital twin with 3D soil blocks then lets farmers see why one rotation is safer.
details:
TRY IT LIVE: https://fieldshift.loanhviet.dev

Open "Ruộng của tôi" (My fields) and pick a sample field. Sóc Trăng reproduces the video (84 vs 177 days, 12/12 scenarios). The model covers the Mekong Delta only.

WHAT IT DOES

FieldShift answers one question for one field: "Which crop sequence should I plant over the next three seasons, and how sure can I be?"

1. Locate and draw. Search for a place on a 3D globe, fly down to satellite imagery and draw the parcel by clicking its corners. GPS and walk-the-boundary are also supported.

2. Field profile. Current rotation, irrigation and drainage. Anything the farmer has not told us is stored as an assumption, never as a farmer-reported fact.

3. Year outlook: "What will next dry season look like?" The app uses the latest NOAA ONI published before the planning date to pick analog years. For 2026–27 the ONI is +2.5 (strong El Niño), with analog years 2015–16 and 2023–24. NASA GPM IMERG shows dry-season rain in those years was about 30% of normal (49 mm vs 161 mm).

4. Rotation engine. The engine generates every rotation that fits the regional crop calendar (rice, maize, soybean, mungbean, peanut, sesame, watermelon, fallow/cover crop; early or standard sowing). It simulates each one day by day with a FAO-56 water balance (ET0 from NASA POWER, crop coefficients, paddy ponding, drainage), adds heat, waterlogging and salinity-overlap rules, and keeps the Pareto-optimal options across 12 scenarios.

5. Decision package. 2–5 conditional strategies sit next to the current practice, each with a robustness score (wins out of 12 scenarios), a confidence level, a plain-language reason, a pre-sowing checklist and field triggers (e.g. "measure canal salinity; if it exceeds the threshold, re-plan").

6. Digital twin and season tracking. Replay two rotations week by week on a shared calendar: cumulative irrigation, the salinity window, stress weeks, and 3D cut-away soil blocks showing canal, ponded water, roots and soil moisture. "What-if" changes sowing dates or water limits. During the season, farmers log measurements and the plan is flagged for re-planning when a trigger fires.

WHY IT MATTERS

The Mekong Delta grows about half of Vietnam's rice. Saline intrusion and El Niño droughts (2015–16, 2019–20) caused major losses, and the official 2026–27 guidance (Công văn 2504/TTTV-TTBVTV) already asks farmers to adjust seasons and switch to upland crops. Farmers receive this as province-wide bulletins. FieldShift turns it into a field-specific, comparable and checkable plan: what to change, under which conditions, and what to measure first.

SCIENTIFIC HONESTY

- No look-ahead: all inputs are restricted to data published before the planning date. CMIP6 is blocked before its 2022 release.

- Forecasts, climate projections, climatology and stress tests are labelled separately and never mixed.

- Source conflicts are explicit: NASA POWER maximum temperature runs 2.8–4.1 °C warmer than ERA5 inland in March. We correct it only for counting hot days and keep the original POWER data for evapotranspiration.

- Evidence in the repo: 13 rules with sources, a sensitivity analysis, backtests on 2016 and 2020 weather, an ENSO hindcast with the right wet/dry direction in 12 of 15 cases, and a full limitations page.

- Limits are stated in the app: grid cells are not field measurements, soil data is missing, salinity dates are assumptions until canal salinity is measured, and value weights are a team heuristic, not a yield model.

TOOLS

Python 3.11, FastAPI, SQLite, pytest (104 tests), React 19, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, three.js, GitHub Actions CI. The demo video is a screen capture of the real app with an AI-generated voice-over (Chatterbox TTS).

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- An ENSO analog-year outlook that answers "Which past year will next dry season look like?" with NASA rainfall evidence, without pretending to be a forecast.

- Rotation planning as a multi-scenario Pareto search, always shown against current practice, instead of a single "best crop".

- A digital twin that only replays engine results, so what farmers see is exactly what was computed.

- "Days crops stand in salt" as a farmer-readable metric, linked to field triggers that make the plan a living document.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Farmers first ask "Do I keep my main rice crop?", so the engine protects the winter–spring rice season. We also considered the official 2026 guidance and regional sowing calendars; missing data, which we show as "unknown" with a checklist instead of inventing it; uncertainty in ENSO signals; the mismatch between grid data and real fields; phone-sized screens and an offline demo; and not overclaiming.
